finding.claim: Broken authorization: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of using require_edit(), so any caller can overwrite the body of any document regardless of owner/editor status. The sibling update_title route correctly uses require_edit.
finding.source: Any authenticated (or otherwise request-reaching) user sending PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...}; doc_id is attacker-chosen path parameter.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20 (write to a protected document).

trace.note: doc = DOCS[doc_id] fetched with no ownership check
can_edit(g.user, doc) return value ignored; no abort(403)
doc body overwritten with attacker-supplied JSON

finding.guards_checked: Checked require_edit (used only in update_title at line 27, not in update_doc); can_edit at line 7 returns a bool but is not enforced; no before_request/decorator auth middleware exists in the file; no other validation on the path.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: can_edit (docs.py:7) returns a bool that is discarded at line 19; require_edit (abort(403)) is only used in update_title at line 27. No before_request or decorator exists.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement with no abort, so docs.py:20 overwrites the body for any caller. By contrast, update_title at docs.py:27 uses require_edit. Caveat: g.user is never set in this directory (the only matches are in docs.py), so it is presumably populated by auth code outside this repo. The attacker is therefore any authenticated low-privilege user.
